nodes.summary: Let $(T, (V_t))$ be a tree-decomposition of a graph $G$ and let $K$ be a finite set of pairwise adjacent vertices of $G$. Then some bag $V_t$ contains $K$.
nodes.title: Every clique lies in a bag

nodes.summary: For every natural number $r$ there is a natural number $k$ such that every finite graph whose tree-width is greater than $k$ has the $r \times r$ grid as a minor. The grid is the box product of two paths on $r$ vertices: its vertices are the pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i, j < r$, and two pairs are adjacent when they differ by one in exactly one coordinate.
nodes.title: Grid theorem (Robertson–Seymour)

nodes.summary: For every natural number $k$, every infinite sequence $G_0, G_1, \dots$ of finite graphs of tree-width at most $k$ has two terms $G_i, G_j$ with $i < j$ such that $G_i$ is a minor of $G_j$: the graphs of bounded tree-width are well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation.
nodes.title: Graphs of bounded tree-width are well-quasi-ordered by minors (Robertson–Seymour)

nodes.summary: Let $H$ be a minor of a finite graph $G$. If $G$ has tree-width at most $k$, then so does $H$. Minors are the relation of graph minors: finite sequences of isomorphisms, vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions.
nodes.title: Tree-width does not increase under taking minors

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a finite graph and $k$ a natural number. Then $G$ has tree-width at most $k$ if and only if $G$ contains no bramble of order greater than $k + 1$.
nodes.title: Tree-width duality theorem (Seymour–Thomas)

nodes.summary: A graph with at most $k + 1$ vertices has tree-width at most $k$: a tree with one node whose bag is the whole vertex set is a tree-decomposition.
nodes.title: The one-bag decomposition

nodes.summary: Every finite tree has tree-width at most one. Root the tree $G$ at a vertex $r$; give each vertex $v$ the bag consisting of $v$ and its parent, the unique neighbour of $v$ closer to $r$ (the root has the bag $\{r\}$). With $G$ itself as decomposition tree these bags satisfy (T1)–(T3) and have at most two vertices.
nodes.title: Trees have tree-width at most one

nodes.summary: Let $V$ be a finite set with $n$ elements. The complete graph on $V$ has tree-width at most $k$ if and only if $n \le k + 1$. Hence $\mathrm{tw}(K_n) = n - 1$ for every $n \ge 1$; for $n = 0$ the statement says that the graph with no vertices has tree-width at most every $k$.
nodes.title: Tree-width of complete graphs

nodes.summary: A graph $G$ has tree-width at most $k$, for a natural number $k$, if it has a tree-decomposition all of whose bags have at most $k + 1$ vertices. The tree-width $\mathrm{tw}(G)$ is the least width of a tree-decomposition, so for a finite graph and $k \ge 0$ this is $\mathrm{tw}(G) \le k$. For a graph with infinitely many vertices the predicate is always false, because the decomposition tree is finite and so are the…
nodes.title: Tree-width at most `k`

nodes.summary: A tree-decomposition $(T, (V_t))$ has width at most $k$ if every bag has at most $k + 1$ vertices. The width of a tree-decomposition is $\max\{|V_t| - 1 : t \in T\}$, so this says that the width is at most $k$.
nodes.title: Width at most `k`

nodes.summary: A bramble in a graph $G$ is a set $\mathcal{B}$ of vertex sets of $G$ such that each member induces a connected subgraph (in particular it is nonempty) and any two members touch.
nodes.title: Bramble

nodes.summary: If a graph has tree-width at most $k$ and $k \le l$, it has tree-width at most $l$.
nodes.title: Tree-width bounds are monotone

nodes.summary: If a graph has an edge $uv$, it does not have tree-width at most $0$: by (T2) some bag contains both $u$ and $v$, so it has at least two vertices.
nodes.title: A graph with an edge has tree-width at least one

nodes.summary: In a graph with at most $k$ vertices no bramble has order greater than $k$: the whole vertex set covers every bramble, because the members of a bramble are nonempty.
nodes.title: Small graphs have no large brambles

nodes.summary: A vertex set covers a bramble $\mathcal{B}$ if it meets every member of $\mathcal{B}$; the order of $\mathcal{B}$ is the least size of a cover. The bramble has order greater than $k$ when no set of at most $k$ vertices covers it.
nodes.title: Bramble of order greater than `k`

nodes.summary: Two vertex sets $X, Y$ of a graph $G$ touch if they have a vertex in common or $G$ has an edge joining a vertex of $X$ to a vertex of $Y$.
nodes.title: Touching vertex sets

nodes.title: Tree-decomposition

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
